source.title: Ensemble of Large Language Models for Curated Labeling and Rating of Free-text Data
source.authors: Jiaxing Qiu; Dongliang Guo; Papini Natalie; Peace Noelle; C. Levinson; Teague R. Henry

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares annotation performance for four 7–8B models with GPT-4o, which bears on downstream performance and model scale, but it does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. when discussing architectural differences, but does not test their loss-scaling results. Its only result bearing on a claim version is the reported GPT-4o versus smaller-model performance comparison in the Reddit annotation task.
record.test_reason: The study proposes an ensemble of four 7–8B open-source LLMs for topic labeling and evaluates it against human labels. It cites Kaplan et al. only in passing. It has no pretraining loss, no scale sweep and no fit. Its only scale-related result compares GPT-4o (parameter count unknown, different family and training) with four same-sized models on one task. That is a single uncontrolled two-point contrast, so it cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. It does not test V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that same-sized small LLMs differ widely in precision and sensitivity. Ensembles of them give the best accuracy against human labels, approaching GPT-4o. Relevancy scores agree more across models than binary labels do. They also remark in passing that parameter size matters for LLM-assisted tasks, but draw no scaling-law conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law recipe, loss measurement, or scaling fit was performed; the study evaluates an LLM ensemble for text annotation.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4o (closed, size unstated) labels eating-disorder topics in Reddit posts more accurately than four 7–8B open models. Its agreement with human annotation is AC1 0.976, Kappa 0.885. The authors say parameter size 'should be considered an important factor.'
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger frontier models outperform small open models on applied annotation tasks (uncontrolled cross-family comparison, not a scaling trend).

record.problems: The scale-related comparison is limited to GPT-4o versus four similarly sized smaller models in one task. The paper gives no exact GPT-4o values in the text and reports no pretraining-loss measurements or scale curve.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed size.
No other modality or training regime.
No graded scale series or relation to pretraining loss. There is only an uncontrolled GPT-4o versus 7–8B comparison on one task.
No fitting choices or exponents examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V6 limits_scope verdict over-reads a single cross-family comparison. It is reclassified as cites_only/T6 with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute sweep, or power-law fit.
No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or parameter/token scaling with compute.
No controlled architecture comparison using loss as the outcome.
No scaling-law test in another modality or training regime.
The paper compares one large-sized model with four similarly sized smaller models in one annotation task; it does not test a graded scale trend or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.size_stated: large-sized; exact parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated labeling performance against human annotations and compared with four smaller open-source LLMs.

conditions.value: Reddit posts; 1,080 human-annotated posts for evaluation
Labeling 15 topics related to eating disorders and dieting
Four open-source models stated to be 7–8 billion parameters

rows.measure: Labeling performance in predicting human annotations; Figure 4 reports F1-score, precision, and sensitivity
rows.baseline: Four open-source 7–8 billion parameter models; exact comparison values figure only
rows.value: Figure only; text says GPT-4o performance was generally higher than that of the selected open-source LLMs
rows.note: This is a single large-model comparison, not a scale sweep. The text provides no exact GPT-4o metric values or evidence that performance follows a predictable curve.
rows.check: GPT-4o versus four 7–8B models of different families on one annotation task. GPT-4o's size is not stated, and model family, training data and closed-versus-open status are confounded with size. The values are figure-only. No scale trend or loss relation can be read, so the row does not measure what V6 names. It is better treated as context; the state 'partial' has no basis.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GPT-4o compared with four 7–8B models on Reddit topic labeling
reader_labels.reason: GPT-4o is reported to perform generally better, but a single large-versus-small comparison does not establish predictable improvement with scale; see r1.
